newsitem.title: UK: Concorde threatens ozone layer, scientists say.
newsitem.headline: Concorde threatens ozone layer, scientists say.

text.p: The supersonic airliner Concorde and subsonic aircraft may be destroying the ozone layer by leaving a fog of sulphuric acid in their wake, the New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) had a research plane trail Concorde as it flew over the ocean near New Zealand, sampling its exhaust fumes 10 minutes after it had passed.
NOAA discovered much more sulphuric acid, in the form of a fog, than expected.

Previously researchers thought most of the sulphur burnt in aircraft engines formed sulphur dioxide. This would gradually convert into sulphuric acid which would then condense onto particles in the air with little impact on stratospheric chemical processes.
But David Fahey of the NOAA said the research on Concorde's emissions showed that the burnt sulphur emerged as sulphur trioxide, which converts much more rapidly to sulphuric acid.
When there is a shortage of particles in the atmosphere for the acid to condense onto, it creates a fog of new particles.
This has an important impact on the ozone layer, because the chlorine pollutants that destroy ozone gather on such particles.

"A fleet of 500 supersonic aircraft like Concorde could double the surface area of tiny particles present in the stratosphere. That would have a direct effect on stratospheric ozone," Fahey told the New Scientist.
He said he feared that while the handful of Concordes currently in service may not pose a big threat, other types of aircraft which fly in the stratosphere may also be doing damage.
"We haven't done the measurements yet, but we see no reason why their emissions should be very different from Concorde," said Fahey.
British Airways and Air France each acquired seven Concordes, the first of which was brought into service in 1976.
Cruising at 1,350 mph, the transatlantic trip takes just 3-1/2 hours, landing passengers in New York before they took off in London in terms of local time.
